read.sections.0.heading.back: Pattern is also the result of skilled work

read.sections.0.text.source:
Clothing can show belonging, ceremony, taste and status. It also serves everyday needs. Indonesian batik brings together design, skilled work and social traditions. Batik is a way of decorating cloth with wax and dye. Its patterned surface comes from decisions about wax, dye and cloth. So a textile records the maker's control of materials as well as a design.

Batik tulis is hand-drawn wax-resist decoration. A resist is a material that protects part of the cloth from dye. The maker uses a tool called a canting, which has a small metal cup and a spout, to guide melted wax onto the cloth. The wax protects chosen areas from the dye. Waxing, colouring, drying and washing are repeated, and a pattern of many colours builds up.

Batik cap uses a patterned copper stamp to put on the wax. Some artisans, or skilled makers, combine stamped designs with hand-drawn details. These methods organise the work differently, even when the finished cloths look just as detailed.
read.sections.0.text.back:

Batik tulis is wax-resist decoration drawn by hand. A resist is a material that protects part of the cloth from dye. The batik maker uses a tool called a canting, which has a small metal cup and a spout, to make melted wax, called malam, flow onto the cloth. The wax protects chosen parts from the dye. Batik cap uses a patterned copper stamp to put on the wax. Some artisans, or skilled makers, combine stamped motifs with details drawn by hand. These ways organise the work differently, even though the finished cloths look just as detailed.
read.sections.0.text.note: Batik terms as used in Indonesia: batik tulis, canting, malam (batik wax, named once, then "lilin"), batik cap, cap. "Perintang" (resist) is the glossary word, from "perintang warna".

Clothes can show who you belong with. They can show a special day or a person's rank. They are also for everyday use. Batik is a way to decorate cloth with wax and dye. In Indonesia, batik joins design, skill and tradition. So a cloth shows the maker's skill, not only a design.

In batik tulis, a maker draws with hot wax. The tool is called a canting. It has a small metal cup and a spout. The wax is a resist. It keeps the dye off some parts of the cloth. The maker waxes, dyes, dries and washes the cloth again and again. Slowly a pattern of many colours grows.

In batik cap, a metal stamp puts on the wax. Some artisans, or skilled makers, use both ways. The work is done in different ways. But the cloths can look just as detailed.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Cloth in family and community life
read.sections.1.heading.back: Cloth in family and community life

read.sections.1.text.source:
Batik also belongs to families and communities. UNESCO, part of the United Nations, describes cloths used to carry babies, clothes worn for work and study, and special cloths for weddings and other occasions. Knowledge often passes from older people to younger ones. Batik patterns have taken in many influences, including calligraphy and designs of flowers and animals. A motif is a shape or picture that repeats in a design. Makers keep adapting their motifs and their work.

In 2009, Indonesian batik was added to UNESCO's list of intangible heritage. Intangible heritage means the knowledge, practices and expressions that people carry and pass on. This recognition is about knowledge and practice. It does not declare one pattern the correct design for everyone.
read.sections.1.text.back:

read.sections.2.heading.source: Two cloths from two parts of Java
read.sections.2.heading.back: Two cloths from two parts of Java

read.sections.2.text.source:
The two museum textiles come from different places in Java. Surakarta, inland in Central Java, was one of the region's royal courts. Its batiks often combine indigo, a deep blue dye, with shades of brown. The late nineteenth-century wrapper shown here arranges six patterns in repeated diagonal bands. Every sixth band has more indigo, so that pattern is easier to see from far away. Colour traditions linked with the court and one maker's careful waxing meet in the same cloth. The museum record does not name its maker or prove that a royal person owned it.

Indramayu, on the north coast of West Java, had its own skilled batik production. The mid-nineteenth-century tubular skirt has a central head section, called a kepala. Around it are closely worked patterns of animals and flowers. Its gold leaf, called prada, suggests that it was worn by a bride. The gold was left off the narrow top part, tucked in at the waist, where it would be hidden or rub away. So this regional craft joined careful waxing, costly decoration and practical knowledge of dressing.

Both places are on the island of Java, but an inland court tradition and a north-coast workshop are not the same. The two cloths show variation within batik. Neither one shows the identity, religion or clothing choices of every Javanese or Indonesian person.

Textiles bring art into histories of work and identity. Makers needed tools, materials, time and skill, and wearers added meaning by using the cloth. A photograph shows a finished surface. Knowing how and where a cloth was made explains some of the work and relationships behind it. It still leaves gaps that a good museum label should admit.
read.sections.2.text.back:
The two cloths from the museum come from different places in Java. Surakarta, inland in Central Java, was one of the royal courts in the region. Surakarta batik often combines indigo, a deep blue dye, with shades of brown. The long cloth from the late 19th century shown here arranges six motifs in repeated slanting bands. Every sixth band has more indigo, so that motif is easier to see from far away. Colour traditions linked with the court and one batik maker's careful waxing meet in the same cloth. The museum's record does not name its maker or prove that the cloth belonged to a member of the royal family.

Indramayu, on the north coast of West Java, had its own skilled batik production. This sarong from the middle of the 19th century has a central part called the kepala. Around it are closely worked motifs of animals and flowers. Its gold layer, called prada, gives a clue that the cloth was worn by a bride. Gold was not put on the narrow top part, which was tucked in at the waist, where gold would be hidden or rub away. So this regional craft combined careful waxing, costly decoration and practical knowledge of how to dress.

Both places are on the island of Java, but the inland court tradition and the craft tradition of the north coast are not the same. The two cloths show the variety within batik. Neither one shows the identity, religion or clothing choices of every Javanese or Indonesian person.

Textiles bring art into histories of work and identity. Makers needed tools, materials, time and skill, and wearers added meaning by using the cloth. A photo shows the finished surface. Knowing how and where a cloth was made explains some of the work and relationships behind it. There are still gaps that a good museum label should admit.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Keraton" for the royal court of Surakarta. "A north-coast workshop" became "tradisi perajin di pesisir utara" (the craft tradition of the north coast), since "pesisir" is how batik writing in Indonesia names north-coast batik. Keep "memberi petunjuk" (gives a clue): the bridal use is the museum's suggestion, not a fact.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
The two cloths come from different parts of Java. Surakarta is inland, in Central Java. It had a royal court. Its batiks often use deep blue and brown. The first cloth was made in the late 1800s. It has six patterns in slanted bands. Every sixth band has more blue. So you can see that pattern from far away. The museum does not know who made it. It cannot prove that a royal person owned it.

Indramayu is on the north coast of West Java. It had its own skilled makers. The second cloth is a skirt shaped like a tube. It was made in the middle of the 1800s. Its central part is called the kepala. Small animals and flowers fill the rest. It has gold leaf, called prada. This suggests that a bride wore it. There is no gold at the top. That part was tucked in at the waist. Gold there would be hidden or rub off.

Both places are on Java. But their traditions are different. A cloth does not show what every Javanese or Indonesian person believes or wears.

A photo shows only the finished cloth. Knowing how and where it was made tells us more. But some gaps stay. A good museum label should say so.

write.prompt.source: Explain how knowing how a cloth was made changes what you can learn from its pattern. Use one step of the making and one way people used or passed on batik. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Explain how knowing how a cloth was made changes what you can learn from its pattern. Use one step of its making and one way people used or passed on batik. Two or three sentences are enough.

write.example.source: The blue bands on the Surakarta wrapper were made by covering parts of the cloth with wax, dyeing it, and doing this again and again. This shows that the pattern took a lot of time and skill, not just a good idea. People also used batik for babies, work and weddings, and older people taught younger ones. But the museum does not know the maker's name, so that part of the story is missing.
write.example.back: The blue bands on the long cloth from Surakarta were made by covering parts of the cloth with wax, dyeing it, and doing this again and again. This shows that the maker needed a lot of time and skill, not just a good idea. People also used batik for babies, work and weddings, and older people taught younger ones. But the museum does not know the maker's name, so that part of the story is missing.
write.example.note: The second sentence follows the Indonesian starter "Ini menunjukkan bahwa pembuatnya ..." (the maker), so it says the maker needed time and skill rather than "the pattern took".

educatorNotes.0.source: The two Javanese cloths don't stand for every community or motif. The bridal use of the Indramayu skirt is the museum's qualified suggestion, and an unnamed maker is a gap in the surviving record, not evidence that no one person made the cloth. Keep the documented making process apart from a tentative interpretation of use.
educatorNotes.0.back: The two Javanese cloths don't stand for every community or motif. The bridal use of the Indramayu sarong is the museum's suggestion with reservations, and an unnamed maker is a gap in the surviving record, not evidence that the cloth was not made by one particular person. Keep the recorded making process apart from the uncertain interpretation of its use.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: the wax and dye stages link the pattern to skill and time; a social connection may be wear, ceremony, trade, teaching between generations, or the gap in the maker's record. Simple English is fine.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for Write: the wax and dye stages link the pattern to skill and time; the social connection may be wear, ceremony, trade, teaching between generations, or the gap in the record about its maker. Simple language is fine.

educatorNotes.2.source: No hot-wax activity is needed, and none should be done without proper supervision. Don't present all patterned commercial cloth as batik, or read a motif's meaning from its look alone.
educatorNotes.2.back: No hot-wax activity is needed, and none should be done without proper supervision. Don't call all factory-made patterned cloth batik, or read a motif's meaning from its look alone.
educatorNotes.2.note: "Commercial cloth" is "kain bermotif buatan pabrik" (factory-made patterned cloth), which is what learners in Jakarta will know as printed "batik".

educatorNotes.3.source: The making process (canting, repeated waxing and dyeing, the copper stamp of batik cap) comes from the Australian Museum's The Batik Process, used as background only. UNESCO's account supports batik as living heritage; the photographs and film on UNESCO's page are separately copyrighted and aren't used.
